title: Paisius Velichkovsky
hookLine: a Ukrainian monk translates the Philokalia into Slavonic and renews Russian monasteries

cards: On Mount Athos, the Holy Mountain in Greece, a monk from Ukraine sits with two texts side by side. One is an old Slavonic translation of a Greek writer on prayer. The other is the Greek itself.
They don't match. Copyists have muddled the Slavonic until some sentences barely make sense.
He had walked out of a theological academy in Kyiv without finishing, not failing, just restless: the lectures were full of argument, and he wanted to learn how to pray.
Now the books his own people pray from turn out to be blurred. So he sets out to learn Greek properly and fix them.

teach.b: Paisius had looked for a living teacher of prayer and, by his own account, mostly failed to find one. So he learned Greek well enough to read the old writers on prayer for himself.
Other monks began gathering around him, first on Athos and later in monasteries in Moldavia, in what is now Romania.
He ran those communities in two languages, so Slavic and Romanian monks could both follow the services and readings. And he gave his life to translation.
Working from Greek manuscripts, he rendered the teachings of the Philokalia into Church Slavonic, the language of worship in the Russian and other Slavic churches.
Now a Russian monk who had never seen Athos could read the desert fathers on watchfulness and the Jesus Prayer. Paisius never went to Russia to lead it himself.
His disciples carried his books and his way of life north, and with them came our line: the startsy.

A starets, in Russian, is an elder, a monk whose long practice of prayer lets him guide others. You go to him, open your heart, tell him your thoughts, and he gives a word for you. It isn't a lecture.
It's a relationship, closer to a doctor and a patient, or a parent and a child.
Paisius taught that obedience to a wise guide protects a beginner on the road into inner prayer, because a beginner left alone easily fools himself.
Through his disciples, elders became a living presence in Russian monasteries, and ordinary people, peasants and nobles, began making journeys to ask them for a word.
The restless student who couldn't find a teacher helped form the teachers who followed.

how: In Orthodox Christianity, people may have a spiritual father or mother, often a priest or monastic, to whom they bring their thoughts and confession, and some travel to monasteries to ask an elder for guidance.

games.q: you're a young monk who wants to learn prayer, but you can't find a living teacher anywhere. what do you do?
o: give up and go back to the academy.
learn from the old writings, and become a teacher yourself.
invent your own method of prayer.
games.why: Paisius dug into old Greek manuscripts on Athos, translated them, and gathered disciples who became elders.

practice: Bring to mind someone older or wiser who has helped you: a grandparent, a teacher, a pastor, a friend who's been through things. Hear their voice, and remember one thing they said that stayed.
If you pray, give thanks for them or pray for them by name; if you don't, just hold them with gratitude.
